[SECTION] ## ORAL ORDER  [PER SMT. V.K. TAHILRAMANI, J.] :

1.Heard learned counsel for the appellant and learned counsel

for the respondent.

2.The question raised by the appellant before this court is as to whether the Family Court in India has got jurisdiction to try the matter involving a foreign citizen whose domicile is outside the territory to which the Hindu Marriage Act extends.

3.The case of the respondent is that she and the appellant are both Hindus and  her marriage with the appellant took place on 03.12.2007 at Pune as per Hindu Vedic Rites.  The respondent filed a petition for divorce and maintenance being P.A. No. 1034 of 2008 before the Family Court at Pune.  By filing Exh. 12, the husband had challenged the jurisdiction of the Family Court at Pune to try and decide the petition on the ground that he was not a domicile of India  and therefore, the petition is barred under Section 1(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act. The Family Court observed that the case of the respondent was that she and the appellant got married at Pune whereas the case of the appellant was that they were married in USA, hence, the Family Court directed the parties to lead evidence if any, in support of their claims only to

the point of marriage.  The said decision was challenged before this  Court.   This  Court  observed  that  the  contention  of  the appellant is that the parties were not at all married whereas the contention of the respondent was that they were married in Pune as per Hindu Vedic Rites.  This Court observed that there was no reason for the appellant to shy away from evidence being led. Observing thus, this Court held that no case was made out to interfere with the said order dated 10.02.2012.  Thereafter, the parties  led  evidence.   After  leading  evidence,  the  matter  was again  heard  by  the  Family  Court.   After  going  through  the evidence led by both the sides, the Family Court held that the marriage had taken place in Pune and in view of Section 19 of the Hindu Marriage  Act, the Family Court at Pune  would  have the jurisdiction to deal with the matrimonial proceedings initiated by the wife and also on the ground that she is residing within the jurisdiction  of the  said Court.   Observing  thus, the  application preferred by the applicant - husband, wherein he has raised the plea that the Family Court at Pune had no jurisdiction, came to be rejected by order dated 05.08.2013.  Hence, this petition.

4.The Family Court, Pune held that it had jurisdiction to decide the case on two grounds.  The main ground is that the evidence shows that the parties were married at Pune as per Hindu Vedic Rites and secondly because the wife was residing at Pune.  There is no dispute that the wife is a resident of Pune.  We now proceed to decide whether the observation of the Family Court that the parties were married in Pune is correct or not.

4.The Family Court, Pune held that it had jurisdiction to decide the case on two grounds.  The main ground is that the evidence shows that the parties were married at Pune as per Hindu Vedic Rites and secondly because the wife was residing at Pune.  There is no dispute that the wife is a resident of Pune.  We now proceed to decide whether the observation of the Family Court that the parties were married in Pune is correct or not.

5.The case of the respondent is that her profile was registered on a matrimonial site which was replied by the appellant.  The appellant's mother and father along with the appellant came from USA to India.  They met the respondent and her parents and they decided to get married.  Engagement ceremony was performed on 12.01.2007 at Sankkalp Mangal Karyalaya, Shashtri Road, Pune. The respondent and his parents left for USA and returned back to India  in  November  2007.   On  02.12.2007,  various  religious ceremonies  were  performed  and  on  03.12.2007,  the  marriage ceremony was performed at Punyaee Sabhagriha at Paud Road,

Kothrud, Pune.  Thereafter, the appellant and the respondent went to Goa for their honeymoon.  After returning back from Goa, the appellant  left  for  USA.   As  per  the  appellant's  direction,  the respondent-wife went to USA on K-1 Visa.

6.The case of the appellant is that the  marriage was never

solemnized  in  India.   In  fact,  it  is  his  case  that  the  marriage between  him  and  the  respondent  never  took  place.   The respondent was in hurry to go to USA and hence, entered the country on K-1 Visa.  The appellant is a citizen of USA.  He has been living in USA since he was two years old.  His schooling and college  education  was  completed  in  USA  and  he  became  the citizen of USA in the year 1982.  Thus, his case is that he is not domiciled in India and therefore, Hindu Marriage Act cannot be made applicable to him.

7.Both the parties have filed documents.  The appellant has relied on  documents to show that no marriage took place in Pune whereas the respondent has filed documents to show that the

marriage took place in Pune on 03.12.2007.  The respondent-wife has  examined  herself.   She  has  also  examined  PW  2  Adwait Dandavate who was the purohit who conducted the  marriage, PW 3 Subhash Panse who is their family friend, PW 4 Santosh Raut - the photographer who took photos and video CD of the marriage ceremony and PW 5 Mrs. Pallavi @ Sayali who is the sister-in-law of  the  respondent.   The  respondent  has  also  relied  on  the photographs and video CD of the marriage, receipt of marriage hall booking, wedding card, copy of  airline tickets to show that she and the appellant had travelled to Goa, boarding pass to Goa and counselor's report etc.

8.The  respondent had deposed that her marriage  with  the appellant was solemnized on 03.12.2007 at Punyaee Sabhagriha, Paud Road, Kothrud, Pune, Maharashtra, India as per the Hindu Vedic Rites.  She has stated that there were 235 invitees of which 159 invitees were from her side.  She has given the names of some of the relatives present during the marriage.  Thereafter, she mentioned about the rites and rituals that took place.    She

has stated that after the marriage, she and the appellant went to Goa for honeymoon.

9. PW 2 Adwait Dandwate is the  Purohit (Priest).  He has stated that he performed the marriage of the appellant and the respondent.   PW  3  Subhash  Panse  is  the  family  friend  of  the respondent.  He has stated that he was acquainted with the family of the respondent since 25 years.  He had attended the marriage function.   He  had  participated  in  buying  ornaments  and purchasing  marriage  material  and  clothes.   He  has  placed  on record  some  photographs  showing  his  participation  in  the marriage of the appellant and the respondent.

has stated that after the marriage, she and the appellant went to Goa for honeymoon.

9. PW 2 Adwait Dandwate is the  Purohit (Priest).  He has stated that he performed the marriage of the appellant and the respondent.   PW  3  Subhash  Panse  is  the  family  friend  of  the respondent.  He has stated that he was acquainted with the family of the respondent since 25 years.  He had attended the marriage function.   He  had  participated  in  buying  ornaments  and purchasing  marriage  material  and  clothes.   He  has  placed  on record  some  photographs  showing  his  participation  in  the marriage of the appellant and the respondent.

10. PW 4  Santosh Raut is the photographer. He has stated that he took the photographs of the alleged marriage. He has stated about  clicking  of  the  photographs  during  Simant  Pujan  and wedding ceremony on 02.12.2007 and 03.12.2007.  He denied having edited the photographs filed on record.

11.PW 5 Pallavi @ Sayali is the sister-in-law of the respondent. She has deposed about the marriage ceremony of the respondent with the appellant on 03.12.2007 at Pune.

It is seen that the respondent has examined herself as well as four other witnesses, however, the appellant did not enter into the witness box nor he examined any witnesses on his behalf.

12.Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submitted  that  no marriage  at  all  took  place  between  the  appellant  and  the respondent and in order to support his contention, he has placed reliance  on  the  affidavit  dated  09.06.2007  executed  by  the respondent for fiancée  visa which is K-1 Visa and also filing of application for marriage licence in USA. He submitted that this shows that no marriage took place in India and it was clearly the intention of the parties to marry in USA, which marriage ultimately did not take place.  In relation to the affidavit dated 09.06.2007, he pointed out that this is an affidavit executed before the Notary by the respondent stating that she is unmarried and she intends to marry the appellant for which she intends to travel to USA on

fiancée visa.  This according to him shows that no marriage took place in Pune.

It is seen that according to the respondent, the marriage ceremony was performed on 03.12.2007 in Pune.    The date of the marriage is after the date when the affidavit dated 09.06.2007 was affirmed.  As on the date of the execution of the affidavit, the respondent was unmarried, the contents of the affidavit at the relevant time may have been true and correct.

13.Thereafter, learned counsel for the  appellant pointed  out that  both  the  appellant  and  the  respondent  preferred  an application for a marriage licence to be issued in USA.  He also pointed out Annexure 'O' which is dated 06.12.2007.  He pointed out that this document is after the alleged marriage took place on 03.12.2007  and  these  two  documents  clearly  show  that  no marriage took place on 03.12.2007 as alleged by the respondent.

As  far as the document Annexure 'O' dated 06.12.2007 is concerned,  it  is  seen  that the  appellant  himself had made  an application to the Bureau of Consular Affairs and the Bureau of

13.Thereafter, learned counsel for the  appellant pointed  out that  both  the  appellant  and  the  respondent  preferred  an application for a marriage licence to be issued in USA.  He also pointed out Annexure 'O' which is dated 06.12.2007.  He pointed out that this document is after the alleged marriage took place on 03.12.2007  and  these  two  documents  clearly  show  that  no marriage took place on 03.12.2007 as alleged by the respondent.

As  far as the document Annexure 'O' dated 06.12.2007 is concerned,  it  is  seen  that the  appellant  himself had made  an application to the Bureau of Consular Affairs and the Bureau of

Consular Affairs had replied to the said application made by the appellant which is clear from the document Annexure 'O'  which mentions  that,  "Our  record  show  that  'you'  filed  the  I-129F petition" and this document is addressed to the appellant.  Thus, it is clear that no application was made by the respondent but in fact, it was the appellant who had made the application and he had shown the respondent's name as her maiden name.    As far as the application for marriage licence is concerned, this was the document required for Visa purpose and the respondent in her evidence has clearly stated that she did not disclose to the USA Consulate that she was married on 03.12.2007 as the appellant had told her that going on fiancée visa was the only option if she had to go to USA with him.  It is, in these circumstances, that the respondent  gave  such  details  in  the  application  for  marriage licence.

14.As stated earlier, the appellant did not enter the witness box nor examined any witnesses on his behalf, however, on perusal of the written statement, we find that he has mentioned therein that

he was shocked to find marriage ceremonies  being performed. This statement clearly shows that the marriage ceremonies were indeed performed in Pune.  Smt. S.B. Jagtap, marriage counsellor, was directed to watch the CD in presence of both the parties and report accordingly.  The counsellor's report (Exh 58) specifically mentions  about  the  ceremonies  of  marriage  performed  on 03.12.2007.   The  report  mentions  about  the  ceremonies  like Mangalashtak, Kanyadan, Holyfire (hom) vidhi, Saptapadi vidhi, Soonmukh vidhi etc were performed.

15.The  specific  case  of  the  respondent  is  that  after  the marriage took place on 03.12.2007, she and the appellant went to Goa for their honeymoon.  The appellant has admitted traveling to Goa with the respondent, adding it was not for honeymoon, and the respondent accompanied him in her maiden name as they were  not  married.   Interestingly  only  the  appellant  and  the respondent  had  left for  Goa.   There  is  no  case  that  both the families had gone for sightseeing.  Only the appellant and the respondent left for Goa, two days  after alleged marriage.   No

Indian  parent  would  let  their    daughter   travel  alone  with proposed groom before marriage, that too at destination like Goa which is crowded with newly married couples.  There is no other inference to draw except that the parties had gone to Goa for honeymoon.

16.The  respondent,  by  way  of  her  oral  and  documentary evidence  has  proved  that  the  marriage  ceremonies  were performed on 03.12.2007 at Pune.  The averment of the appellant in his written statement that he was shocked to find marriage ceremonies being performed also supports the respondent's case that marriage was indeed performed in Pune.  According to the appellant, he did not know Marathi, hence, he did not know what rituals were going on, however, whether he knew the language or not is immaterial.  The appellant is a major and able to take his own decisions.  What is most relevant to note is that he was accompanied by his parents who understood Marathi culture and ceremonies.  Thus, from the evidence on record, it can be said that the observation of the Family Court that the marriage of the

appellant and the respondent took place in Pune on 03.12.2007 is correct.

appellant and the respondent took place in Pune on 03.12.2007 is correct.

17.Learned counsel for the appellant again  reiterated that the appellant being domiciled in USA, the Hindu Marriage Act is not applicable  to  him.  He  contended  that  the  Court  in  India  has absolutely no jurisdiction to take up the matter involving a Foreign Citizen.  According  to  the  learned  counsel,  the  domicile  of  the appellant is United States of America and so long as he has no domicile  in  India  and  continues  to  be  a  Foreign  Citizen,  the question of invoking the jurisdiction by a party before the Courts in  India  does  not  arise. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant submitted that as the appellant has been living in USA since he is 2 & 1/2 years old and he is a citizen of USA since the year 1982, the  Family  Court  in  Pune  would  have  no  jurisdiction  as  he  is domiciled  in  USA.   To  support  this  contention,  he  has  placed reliance on Section 1 of the Hindu Marriage Act.  As per Section 1 of the  Hindu  Marriage  Act, the  Act is  applicable  to all  Hindus domiciled in the territories to which this Act extends.  The learned

counsel for the appellant submitted that though the appellant is a Hindu,  he  is  not  domiciled  in  the  territory  to  which  this  Act extends as he is domiciled in USA, hence, the petition of the wife before the Family Court, Pune is not maintainable.

18.It is not disputed that the respondent is a citizen of India and domiciled in India.  It is also not disputed that the   appellant was a citizen of India before he was granted USA citizenship in the year 1982.  The law attributes to every person at birth a domicile which  is  called  a  domicile  of  origin.   This  domicile  may  be changed, and a new domicile which is called a domicile of choice, acquired; but the two kinds of domicile differ in one respect.  The domicile  of origin is received by operation of law at birth; the domicile of choice is acquired later by the actual removal of an individual  to  another  country  accompanied  by  his  animus manendi.   The  appellant  admittedly  being  a  Hindu,  if  he  has solemnized the marriage by Hindu Vedic rites in Pune, India, then impliedly,  he  has  submitted  himself  to  the  jurisdiction  of  this Court.   By  marrying  in  India  as  per  the  provisions  of  Hindu

Marriage  Act,  the  appellant  cannot  escape  putting  forth  his domicile.

19.In the instant case, the respondent undoubtedly acquired US citizenship in 1982.  On the date of marriage and date of filing of petition, he was US citizen.  He was time being domiciled in USA, but the domicile of origin i.e of India stuck to him all the time ready for revival the moment respondent intended to return to his roots.   The  possession  by  the  family  of  residential  flat  at Kothrud,Pune and marrying an Indian girl shows his intention to return to his roots.

20.Admittedly, the respondent is an Indian citizen domiciled in India whereas the appellant is USA citizen, domiciled in USA.  The Hindu  Marriage  Act  is  applicable   to  those  persons  who  are 'Hindus' domiciled in the territories to which this Act extends.  If this provision is merely read into the present proceeding, then the appellant will not be within the ambit of the provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act and the jurisdiction of the Family Court at

Pune  will  be  expressly  barred.   The  Hindu  Marriage  Act  is applicable to all Hindus.  Admittedly, both the parties herein are Hindus.   Their  marriage  was  solemnized  as  per  Hindu  Vedic traditions and the marriage is not barred by any clause under Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act.  Section 19 of the Hindu Marriage Act provides the local limits of the Court wherein petition

can be filed.  In the present case, the respondent resides in Pune

and therefore, the petition can be filed in Pune.   Section 19 of the

Hindu Marriage Act reads as under:-

19.  Court to which the petition shall be presented - Every petition under this Act shall be presented to the District Court within the local limits of whose ordinary original civil Jurisdiction -

i.the marriage was solemnized, or

ii.the respondent, at the time of the presentation of the petition, resides, or

iii. the parties to the marriage last resided together, or

[(iii-a) in case the wife is the petitioner, where she is residing on the date of

presentation of the petition, or]

iv. the petitioner is residing at the time of the presentation of the petition, in a case where the respondent is, at that time, residing outside the territories to which this Act extends, or has not been heard of as being alive for a period of seven years or more by those persons who would naturally have heard of him if he were alive]case where the respondent is, at that time, residing outside the territories to which this Act extends, or has not been heard of as being alive for a period of seven years or more by those persons who would naturally have heard of him if he were alive]

[SECTION] ## 21.It was found that the earlier provision regarding jurisdiction

caused  serious  prejudice  to  the  cause  of  women.  It  was  not possible for a women to initiate proceedings before the Court in whose  jurisdiction  she  was  residing.  Because  of  this  rigid

provision,  women  were  compelled  to  approach  the  Courts  in whose jurisdiction the marriage was solemnized or the husband resides or the parties to the marriage last resided together. They have  to  approach  Courts  in  distant  places  to  resolve  their matrimonial disputes. Courts were flooded with transfer petitions to transfer those proceedings on various grounds so as to enable the  wife  to  contest  the  proceedings  before  the  nearest  court without any kind of difficulties. The jurisdiction clause as it stood originally,  was  really  unfair  to  the  women.  Accordingly  it  was decided to amend Section 19 for the purpose of incorporating a provision to enable the wife to file a petition before the District Court in whose jurisdiction she is actually residing. This provision was inserted by Act 50 of 2003 with effect from 23 December, 2003.  Therefore  the  wife  is  now  entitled  to  file  a  matrimonial petition before the District Court in whose territorial jurisdiction she is residing.

22.The Hindu Marriage Act applies to all Hindus domiciled in the territory to which the act extends. Section 19 gives a right to

the wife to present the petition to the District Court within whose jurisdiction she is residing.  When the wife was given the right to initiate the proceedings before the local District Court where she is actually residing, such a provision cannot be defeated by taking a technical plea that no such proceeding would lie on account of Foreign  Citizenship  of  the  husband  or  his  domicile  in  another country.   The  domicile  or  citizenship  of  the  opposite  party  is immaterial  in  a  case  like  this.  In  case  the  marriage  was solemnized under Hindu Law the marital relationship is governed by the provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act. Therefore, Section 19 has to be given a purposeful interpretation. It is the residence of the wife, which determines the question of jurisdiction, in case the proceeding was initiated at the instance of the wife.

23.While considering a provision like Section 19 (iii-a) of the Hindu Marriage Act, the objects and reasons which prompted the parliament to incorporate such a provision has also to be taken note  of.  Sub  Clause  (iii-a)  was  inserted  in  Section  19  with  a specific purpose. Experience is the best teacher. The Government

found the difficulties faced by women in the matter of initiation of matrimonial  proceedings.  The  report  submitted  by  the  Law Commission  as  well  as  National  Commission  for  Women, underlying  the need for such amendment so as to enable the women  to  approach  the  nearest  jurisdictional  court  to  redress their  matrimonial  grievances,  were  also  taken  note  of  by  the Government. Therefore such a beneficial provision meant for the women of our Country should be given a meaningful interpretation by Courts.

24.When the marriage was solemnized under the Hindu law, the proceedings for divorce has also to be made under the said Act. The appellant cannot take any exception to the proceedings in India under the provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act, merely on account of his US citizenship or domicile.

25.The moot question to be decided is as to whether the Indian Courts  have  jurisdiction  to  decide  matrimonial  proceedings involving two Hindus governed by the Hindu Marriage Act even in

cases where the opposite party is a foreign national having his domicile outside India.  The same question arose for consideration before the Supreme Court in the case of Y. Narasimharao Vs Y. Venkatalakshmi[1].  This case was before amendment iii-a was introduced.   In  the  said  case,  the  marriage  was  as  per  the provisions of Hindu Marriage Act, however, the decree of divorce was granted by the Court at Missouri, USA.  The Supreme Court held that the Court at Missouri had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition under the Hindu Marriage Act.  The  relevant observations for the purpose of the present proceedings reads thus:-

7.  Under the provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955  (hereinafter referred to as the  'Act') only the District Court within the local limits of whose original civil jurisdiction (i) the marriage was solemnized, or (ii) the respondent, at the time of the presentation of the petition resides, or (iii) the parties to the marriage last resided together, or (iv) the petitioner is residing at the time of the presentation of the petition, in a case where the respondent is, at the time, residing outside the territories to which the Act extends, or has not been heard of as being alive for a period of seven 1955  (hereinafter referred to as the  'Act') only the District Court within the local limits of whose original civil jurisdiction (i) the marriage was solemnized, or (ii) the respondent, at the time of the presentation of the petition resides, or (iii) the parties to the marriage last resided together, or (iv) the petitioner is residing at the time of the presentation of the petition, in a case where the respondent is, at the time, residing outside the territories to which the Act extends, or has not been heard of as being alive for a period of seven

1(1991)3 SCC 451

years of more by those persons who would naturally have heard of him if he were alive, has jurisdiction to entertain the petition. The Circuit Court of St. Louis Country,  Missouri  had,  therefore,  no  jurisdiction  to entertain  the  petition  according  to  the  Act  under which admittedly the parties were married.

................

17.The marriages which take place in this country can  only  be  under  either  the  customary  or  the statutory law in force in this country. Hence, the only law that can be applicable to the matrimonial disputes is the one under which the parties are married, and no other law........

21. ........   The  parties do and ought to know their rights  and  obligations  when  they  marry  under  a particular  law.   They  cannot  be  heard  to  make  a grievance  about it later or allowed to bypass it by subterfuges as in the present case.

................

17.The marriages which take place in this country can  only  be  under  either  the  customary  or  the statutory law in force in this country. Hence, the only law that can be applicable to the matrimonial disputes is the one under which the parties are married, and no other law........

21. ........   The  parties do and ought to know their rights  and  obligations  when  they  marry  under  a particular  law.   They  cannot  be  heard  to  make  a grievance  about it later or allowed to bypass it by subterfuges as in the present case.

In the case of Narasimha Rao (supra), the Supreme Court

categorically stated that marriages performed under the Hindu

Marriage Act can be dissolved only under the said Act. Naturally, the provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act with regard to jurisdiction

would also come into play. In addition, Section 19 clearly gives jurisdiction  to  the  Court  to  deal  with  matrimonial  proceedings initiated by the wife, if she is residing within the jurisdiction of the said  Court.  There  is  no  question  of  the  respondent  initiating divorce proceedings before the Court at United States of America invoking the provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act. The moment the appellant has married the respondent in India as per Hindu Vedic Rites i.e under the Hindu Marriage Act, he has subjected himself to the jurisdiction of the Court designated to deal with matrimonial disputes under Section 19 of the Hindu Marriage Act.

26.The  marriage  between the  appellant  and  the  respondent could be resolved only on the grounds set out under Section 13 of the  Hindu  Marriage  Act.  The  appellant  has  no  case  that  the application for divorce could be made before the Court at  USA  on the grounds found mentioned in the Hindu Marriage Act.  In such circumstances,  it  would  be  impossible  for  the   respondent  to initiate divorce proceedings before the Court at  USA  on the basis of the averments found in the petition for divorce.

27.We  have  already  held  that  the  marriage  between  the appellant  and  the  respondent  was  solemnized  in  Pune  on 03.12.2007.  In such case, this case would fall under clause i and clause iii-a of  Section 19.  Section 19 of the Hindu Marriage Act clearly gives jurisdiction to the Court to deal with matrimonial proceedings in whose jurisdiction the marriage was solemnized.  It also gives jurisdiction to the Court to deal with the matrimonial proceedings  initiated  by  the  wife  if  she  is  residing  within  the jurisdiction of the Court.    It is not possible / practicable for the respondent to file petition before the US Court. In the case of Surinder Kaur Sandhu Vs. Harbax Singh Sandhu & Anr.[2], the Supreme Court has observed that it is the duty and function of the Court to protect the wife against the burden of litigating in an inconvenient forum.   The   respondent   has   no   support         in USA and she was always an Indian citizen domiciled in       India. Her travel to USA on fiancée visa after marriage in December 2007 can be held as act of an innocent mind and excessive belief in her husband.  It will be unfair to ask her to travel to hostile territory only to redress her grievance.

28.Therefore on a true construction of Section 19 read with Sections  1  and  2  of  the  Hindu  Marriage  Act,  we  are  of  the considered view that the Family court at Pune has got jurisdiction to try the matrimonial litigation initiated by the  respondent not withstanding  the  fact  that  the  appellant  is  a  citizen  of  United States of America and not an ordinary resident of India.

29.In view of above, especially Section 19 of the Act,  we are of the  opinion  that  the  Family  Court  was  right  in  rejecting  the application  of  the  appellant.   In  this  view  of  the  matter,  no interference is called for.  The Family Court Appeal is dismissed.

30.No order as to costs.

[SHRI. P.N. DESHMUKH, J ]       [SMT. V.K. TAHILRAMANI, J ]jfoanz vkacsjdj

P.C.

Heard.

2The petitioner was externed under an order No. 19 of 2011 dated 28/3/2011 for a period of two years from Pune Rural District and Area of Pune Police Commissionerate.  The petitioner preferred an appeal against the said order, which came to be dismissed by the State, by an order dated 10/4/2012.

WP3543.13

3The learned counsel for the petitioner raised two grounds.  The petitioner in one of the cases was acquitted in the offence vide C.R. No. 142 of 2005 of Wanavadi Police Station, for offences u/s 302 r/w 34 of IPC.  The second ground is that in  the  externment  proceedings  reliance  was  placed  by  the externing authority on C.R. No. 90 of 2010.  The said  C.R. was again relied upon by the externing authority.  The learned counsel placed reliance on two judgments in support of his submissions.  He has submitted that the impugned orders are erroneous.  They suffer from non application of mind.4The  learned  APP  has  supported  the  order  of

externment.   It  was  submitted  on  behalf  of  State  that  to highlight the incidents, a list of 28 cases lodged against the petitioner was mentioned in the externment order but in fact the externing authority had placed reliance only on three criminal cases  which  included  C.R.  No.  90  of  2010  registered  in Hadapsar Police Station and other two criminal cases registered

WP3543.13

at Wanavadi Police Station.  These police stations fall under the Pune City jurisdiction.   Considering the activities, statements recorded, the authorities had passed appropriate orders.

5We have perused the order passed by the externing authority and the order passed by the appellate authority.  We have also perused the judgment cited (supra).

6In respect of the first contention of the petitioner, we find that a list of 28 cases was mentioned in the order to demonstrate the fact that these cases were lodged against the petitioner but for the purposes of the present externment order, reliance was placed on three criminal cases.  The criminal case in which according to the petitioner, he was acquitted, was not the basis for externing the petitioner.

7We find that the petitioner was externed from Pune City and District jurisdiction of Pune.  In that we do not notice the order of externment was excessive in nature.  Both the authorities  had  considered  the  record  and  have  passed

WP3543.13

appropriate  orders.   In  exercise  of  our  extraordinary  writ jurisdiction, we are not inclined to interfere with the impugned orders.

8The petition is dismissed.

[TITLE] # IN THE HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT BOMBAY CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION

P.C.:

Rule.  Rule made returnable forthwith.  Respondents waive service.

2.By this petition, the Petitioner challenges the order passed by the School Tribunal, Kolhapur, dismissing his appeal by judgment and order dated 30 January 2013.

3.The Tribunal has dismissed the appeal filed by the Petitioner on two grounds, firstly, that the Petitioner was not appointed after following the due procedure laid down in Section 5 read with Rule 9 of Maharashtra Employees of Private Schools Act and Rules and, secondly, that the post on which the Petitioner was appointed was not a sanctioned post.

bsb                                                2

4.The learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that, as regard the first issue regarding the validity of the appointment, it was not raised by the Respondent management neither by the Deputy Director who had filed reply before the Tribunal.  The Tribunal has suo moto considered the same.  He submitted that the Tribunal has not considered various legal and factual aspects while deciding the said issue.  The learned counsel submitted that this Court in the decisions in the case of  Nita Ramesh Danane  v/s  Dombivali  Mitra  Mandal  &  ors.,reported  in2009(1) Mh.L.J. 796;and Jagdamba Education Society, Nagpur v/s Rajendra s/o Baburao Golhar & ors.,reported in2009(2) Mh.L.J. 522, indicate that no advertisement is necessary for open category post.  He also submitted that there is no requirement for issuance of an advertisement if the post is not sanctioned.  The learned counsel for the management accepted the position that the stand that the Petitioner was not appointed as per procedure, was not taken before the Tribunal.  He submitted that the only ground on which the Petitioner was terminated was that the post was not sanctioned.

5.As regard the post not being sanctioned, the learned counsel for the Petitioner has placed on record a Government Resolution dated 21 May 2014  which,  according  to  him,  sanctions  896  posts  in  the  State  of Maharashtra, including the one held by the Petitioner in the Respondent school. Perusal of the Government Resolution indicates that it has not yet been brought in force and it will be brought in force when requisite funds available.  It is also stated therein that while granting approval to the teachers in respect of the additional sanctioned posts whether they have been  appointed  after  following  due  procedure  of  law  needs  to  be

bsb                                                3

6.The benefit of the Government Resolution cannot be straight way given to the Petitioner, firstly, because it is not yet been brought into force and secondly, there is a finding of the Tribunal that the Petitioner was not appointed  after  following  proper  procedure.   However,  the  various submissions on legal factual aspects made by the learned counsel have not been considered.  Without holding at this stage as to whether the arguments are valid or otherwise, in peculiar facts and circumstances that the post is now sanctioned and the Respondent management is not averse, the matter needs to be remanded back to the Tribunal to reconsider the issue as to whether the Petitioner was appointed as per law.  The learned counsel for the management is also not averse to remand of the petition to the School Tribunal for adjudication of this dispute.

7.Accordingly, the writ  petition is  disposed  of  by quashing and setting aside the impugned order passed on 30 January 2013 and the appeal filed by the Respondent is restored to the file.

7.Accordingly, the writ  petition is  disposed  of  by quashing and setting aside the impugned order passed on 30 January 2013 and the appeal filed by the Respondent is restored to the file.

8.The Tribunal will decide the issue as to whether the Petitioner was appointed by following legal and factual procedure.

9.All contentions of the parties are kept open.  The Respondent management will make the record available to the Tribunal to enable it to arrive at this finding.  Depending upon the decision of the Tribunal, it will be open to the Petitioner to apply to the Deputy Director.  If such an application is made, obviously it will be decided as per law.

10.The Tribunal will consider giving priority to the disposal of the appeal depending upon the schedule of the time bound matters and other commitments.

11.It  will  be  open  to  the  Petitioner  to  place  the  Government Resolution dated 21 May 2014 on record of the appeal along with the requisite amendments.  It will be open to the respondents to file their additional reply.

[SECTION] ## ORDER

These petitions seek to question the denial ofapproval of admissions to the PB BSc (N) course. Thebackground is as follows:

ThepetitionersaI €students|oT thethirdrespondent college studying in PB BSc(Nursing) coursefor the academic year 2012-13. By a notification dated23.05.2012 the Rajiv Gandhi University of HealthSciences had issued admission calendar of events for/the PB BSC(N) course for the academic year 2012-13. —The notification mandated that the Principals of colleges"should submit online admission statement of the'students admitted to their colleges, to the secondrespondentUniversitybetween05.10.2012|and15.12.2012. Thereafter the hard copies of admission

statements along with relevant documents in originalwere to be submitted to the second respondent by18.19.9012 which date was thereafter extended to31.12.2012. Though most colleges adhered to thecalendarOT events 1t_transpiresthat|thethird respondent college had not submitted the necessarydocuments in terms of the notification and the reason|assigned did not convince the University. The Universitywas of the opinion that such non-compliance was aeross negation of academic discipline. However, itconvened a meeting of the erring institutions, includingthe third respondent institution, on 14.08.2013 where itwas indicated that any discrepancy found in theadmission statements would result in the students’!admission not being approved. And the Universityprovisionally permitted the students admitted to appearfor the examination held from 21.08.2013 onwards.But it was on a condition that the results of the'

examination of such students would be announced|subject to the approval of the admission.

It is the case of the University that the institutionhad failed to comply with the directions and failed tosubmit the admission statements in time. Thoughdocuments were sought to be submitted belatedly thesame was not taken into account since the Universityhad already taken a decision not to approve theadmissions of those students whose papers had notbeen submitted. Though the discrepancies, that werenoticed by the University, having been subsequentlycorrected,the Universityhadnotapprovedthe|admissions of the students since the documents were|not furnished in time. Itis on a matter of principle thatthe University has refused to approve the admissions. —It is in this background that the petitioners are beforethis court.

It was certainly well within the discretion of theUniversity to deny the approval of admission as there isclearly a default on the part of the institutions. This,however, should not result in the career of the studentsbeing jeopardized. The need for adherence to the timeschedules and to fall in line with measures to maintaindiscipline imposed by the University cannot be overlooked and be permitted to be followed only in thebreach. This has to be brought home to the respectiveinstitutions. Therefore, the institution ought to beappropriately penalized, aS a reminder to prevent theinstitutions from repeating such indiscretion and laxityon their part. Accordingly, the third respondentinstitution is liable to pay a penalty ofd.2,000/- (Rupees Two Thousand only) for every student whose admissionwas pending approval on account of non-submission ofthe papers by the institutions. On payment of such fee,which shall not be passed on to the students by the

institution, which shall exclusively bear the lhability. —The second respondent University shall grant approvalof admissions on such payment of penalty if everythingis found to be in order. With this observation the'|petitions stand allowed.

The second respondent University is directed toapprove the admission of the petitioners/students andannounce the result immediately since the nextexamination is due on 08.04.2014 and hence the'petitioners shall also be accommodated to take thesupplementary examination if they have failed in anysubject apart from the next year’s examination. If thereis any default on the part of the institution in the futurethe University may take such stringent action aS may bewarranted in its discretion and it shall not be open tothe institutions thereafter to approach this court in thatregard.

the truck was also almost burnt to ashes leavingbehind steel wires of tyres and mass of burnt rubber. —The driver and cleaner of the truck jumped from thetruck and saved their lives but the driver oft thetractor was burnt alive and died on the spot. Theaccident news was also published in the _ locahewspapel, spotSurveyWasconductedandphotographs of the truck which was involved in theaccident were taken. However 845 numbers of thetubes of various sizes could be saved though theywere also affected with fire and loss of Rs.17,37,600/-.aiter salvage were assessed by the Surveyor. Theypleaded that under the circumstances, they did notfind any lapses on their part as they were never atany point of time guilty of any negligence orcarelessness and the same is corroborated by thereport of the Surveyor also on the request of theparties, damage certificate was issued to lodge theclaim with the under writers. They also enclosed asurvey report which clearly gave a graphic description

of the nature of the accident, loss sustained, totalvalue of the goods and aiter deducting salvage valuetotal loss of damage was assessed at Rs.17,37,600/-.When the defendant in categorical terms furnished allthe particulars to the second plaintiff to enable themto claim damages from the Insurance Company, onsuch claim being made, the Insurance Company paidthe said amount. Thereafter, the second plaintiff hasissued a letter of subrogation and also power ofattorney authorising the first plaintiff to get the saidamount. All these documents are not in dispute. |Therefore, the said evidence clearly establishes thatthe second plaintiff had insured the consignment withthe first plaintiff and he put forth a claim, the claimhas been honoured and thereafter a letter ofsubrogation is issued along with Power of Attorney.In the light of this material on record, mere non-production of policy of insurance would, in no way,vitiate the claim put forth by the claimant and

therefore, we do not see any merit in the saidcontention.

[SECTION] ## Point No.2

11. Insofar as mandatory requirement of Section 10 of Carriers Act is concerned, the Section reads asunder:

“10. Notice of loss or injury to be|given within six months.-- No suit shallbe instituted against a common carrier forthe loss of, or injury to 4 [goods includingcontainer, pallets or similar article oftransportused TOconsolidategoodsentrusted| to him for carriage, unless—notice in writing of the loss or injury has_been given to him before the institution ofthe suit and within six months of the timewhen the loss or injury first came to theknowledge of the plaintiff.” —

In the instant case, the accident took place on|9.6.2007. On coming to know about the accident andburning of the entire consignment, the secondplaintiff issued a letter to the defendant requesting

-1/-.

them to reimburse Rs.18,12,160.58 paise. In otherwords, it is a notice in writing of the loss or injurysustained by the second plaintiff. On receipt of thesaid notice, the defendant on 23.7.2007 sent a replyas per Ex.P.6 referring to the said letter forwardingthe documents such as FIR copy/panchanama,photographs of the spot of accident, Stock TransferInvoice, Survey report, damage certificate, LR copy,receipt of survey fees paid by them to osri.RajivKuldiwar, insurance surveyor to enable the secondplaintiff to claim the losses from the Insurance.Company. This notice and reply are all within sixmonths from the date of the accident. Therefore, themandatory requirement of a notice in writing of thelosses or injury has been duly given by the plaintiffsand acknowledged by the defendant and it is too latein the day to contend that, mandatory requirement ofsection 10 of the Carriers Act is not complied with.The trial Court has rightly negatived the saidcontention by a considered order referring to the

aforesaid exhibits. Therefore, we do not see anyjustification to interfere with the said finding.

[SECTION] ## Point NO.3

12. Insofar as grant of interest is concerned, thesuit 1s one for recovery of damages. The plaintiff No.1has claimed interest at 12% per annum from the dateof the petition till realisation. The claim is based onlegal notice issued prior to institution of the suit bythe Insurance Company as per Ex.P.11. Therefore,even in the absence of any contract or agreementbetween the parties under the provision of the InterestAct, plaintiff NO.1 would be entitled to claim interest.However that claim could be upto the date of thedecree. After the date of the decree in the absence ofany trade agreement between the parties, the interestpayable is only at 6% per annum till payment. |Therefore, the same has to be modified. Hence, wepass the following:

- 19 -.

[SECTION] ## ORD BR

The appeal is allowed in part. the judgment and)decree dated 12.11.2010 passed in O.S.No.72/09 onthe file of IV Additional Senior Civil Judge, Mysore, isconfirmed except to the extent of reducing the interestfrom 12% to 6% per annum from the date of thedecree till the date of payment with proportionatecosts.

THIS APPEAL IS FILED UNDER SECTION 260-AOF INCOME TAX ACT, F1961 ARISING OUT OF ORDER)DATED PASSED IN ITA NO.202/BNG/2008, FOR THEASSHSSMENTYRAR2004-2005|PRAYINGTOFORMULATE THE SUBSTANITAL QUESTIONS OF LAW.STATED THEREIN AND TO ALLOW THE APPBAL AND|

SET ASIDB THR ORDER PASSBD BY THR ITAT|BANGALORE IN ITA NO.262/BNG/2008.

THIS APPBAL COMING ON FOR HBARING THISDAY, N KUMAR J., DELIVERED THE FOLLOWING:

[SECTION] ## JUDGMENT

The assessee has preferred this appeal challengingthe findings recorded by the three authorities that theexplanation rendered to explain the undisclosed sourceof investment in business is not acceptable and bringinginto tax the amount under Section 69A of the Income§Tax Act, 1961.

2. The appeal was admitted to consider thefollowing substantial questions of law at the time ofadmission on 08.04.2009:

1. Whether in law, the provisions of section69A of the Act were applicable to the’appellant’s case and the addition of Rs.5lakhs as confirmed by the Tribunal wassustainable?

2. Whether in law, the appellant is said to'have discharged the onus of proving thesource of investment when the appellant’s|mother confirmed the gifts made to her son-the appellant, and the veracity of herstatement having not been disproved by theassessing officer?

3. Whether in law, on mere surmises andsuspicion the Tribunal could sustain the|addition when the appellant had adducedevidence which has not been controverted byany authorities below under the Act?”

3. Learned counsel for the parties have beenheard.

4. The undisputed facts which emerge from thematerial on record is that the assessee’s father died in)January 2002 living behind his widow 1.e., the mother ofthe assessee and the assessee himself. The widow|inherited 6 acres and 20 guntas of agricultural land andshe was also owning 2.607 acres of land in her name. Allthese lands are situated in Chittor in Andhra Pradesh.The case of the assessee was that his mother was)cultivating the land and growing paddy, sugarcane,esround nut and pulses in these lands. It is from theaforesaid crops, she had saved Rs.5.00 lakhs cash andhad kept in the house. That amount was given to himby way of gift which he invested as capital in hisbusiness. The three authorities have concurrently held

the mother was aged about 69 years on the date ofdeath of her husband. Till the death of her husband,the land belonged to her husband, so any incomederived there from rightfully belonged to the husband.There is no material on record to show the income§derived from the lands which was in the hands of the!assessee. If in January 2002, the mother became theowner of 6 acres 20 guntas of agricultural land and sheowned 2.607 acres in her own name, when she is said tohave paid the said amount on 10.04.2003 and15.06.2003, roughly one year after the death of herhusband, it is difficult to believe the case of the.assessee that she had Rs.5.00 lakhs cash kept in thehouse being the income derived from the said land.Therefore, on appreciation of entire evidence on record,three fact finding authorities have carefully held thatthe assessee has failed to prove the said income ofRs.o.00 lakhs in the hands of his mother and paymentof that by way of gift to him. The question whether themother had Rs.5.00 lakhs on the day she is said to havesifted to the son, is purely a question of fact. When

three fact finding authorities on the basis of legalevidence have held that the said fact is not proved, nosubstantial question of law as framed by this Court atthe time of admission arises for consideration at the’hands oft this Court.

Oo. We do not find any error in the findingsrecorded by the three authorities. Therefore, we do notsee any merit in this appeal. Appeal is dismissed.Question of answering the substantial question of lawdo not arise.

Brn

od/-

JUDGE

Sd/-

JUDGE.

[SECTION] ## …

O R D ER (O R AL)

PER J.K. MAHESHWARI, CJ

This appeal arising out of order dated 24.10.2019 passed in Excise Appeal No. 75003 of 2017 with Excise Appeal No. 75004 of 2017 by the Customs, Excise & Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Eastern Zonal Bench, Kolkata (for short, CESTAT) is filed by the Appellant.  2. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Respondent has raised preliminary objections inter alia contending that the value as involved in the present case is of Rs.63.00 lakhs, however, as per National Litigation Policy dated 22.08.2019, if value of any appeal is less than Rupees One Crore, the appeal to the High Court is not maintainable. Second objection is raised that the present matter pertains to refund of Education Cess and Higher Education Cess which were paid along with Excise Duty, however, the said subject matter covers Section 35L and not under Section 35G of the Central Excise Act, 1944 (for short, the Act), therefore, this appeal is not maintainable before the High Court.

3. On the other hand, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant-Revenue has made an attempt to satisfy this Court that the appeal under Section 35G of the Act is maintainable because the order passed by the CESTAT is illegal and passed prior to the subsequent judgment of Supreme Court in the case of M/s Unicorn Industries vs. Union of India and Others in Civil Appeal No. 9237 of 2019 arising out of S.L.P (C) No.21622 of 2012, on 06.12.2019, therefore, this appeal is maintainable.

4. After hearing the learned counsel for both the parties, we find much substance in the preliminary objections as raised by the learned counsel representing the Respondent.

5. At present learned counsel representing the Appellant-Revenue facing difficulty regarding agreed proposal made before the CESTAT of applicability of the judgment of the SRD Nutrients Private Ltd. Vs.CCE, reported in 2017 (TIOL) 416 (S.C.) and relying on the same the order was passed. Later the said judgment has been modified by the Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of M/s

Unicorn Industries vs. Union of India and Others(supra).  However, the counsel for the Appellant-Revenue requests for filing a petition for rectification before the CESTAT, the said prayer appears to be justifiable.

6. In view of the foregoing, we dispose of this appeal, as requested by the counsel representing the Appellant-Revenue with a liberty to take appropriate recourse of law for rectification of the order of the CESTAT.

[TITLE] # Review Pet. (C) No. 01/2020

D.B. THAPA  PETITIONER (S) VERSUS URBAN DEVELOPMENT & HOUSING DEPARTMENT RESPONDENT (S)

For Petitioner : Mr. Yam Kumar Subba, Advocate For Respondent  : Dr. Doma T. Bhutia,

[SECTION] ## Date: 17/03/2021

[SECTION] ## CORAM :

[SECTION] ## HON’BLE MR. JUSTICE JITENDRA KUMAR MAHESHWARI, CJ. HON’BLE MR. JUSTICE BHASKAR RAJ PRADHAN, J.

…

PER J.K. MAHESHWARI, CJ

Being aggrieved by the Order dated 26.11.2020 passed in W.A No. 04 of 2020, this petition has been preferred seeking review.

Learned Counsel for the appellant has raised three points (i) any house construction on the road side is required to compulsorily construct a garage in the house on the land, (ii) it is further contended that in all the houses situated in the road side are having garage, out of them several persons have constructed the garage on the Government land and (iii) the notice for demolition suffers with inherent defects without specifying the violation of any of the provisions of the Sikkim Allotment of House sites and Construction of Building (Regulation and Control) Act, 1985, therefore, there is an error apparent on the face of the record in the order under review, which warrants interference in this petition.

On the other hand learned Additional Advocate General argued in support of the Orders passed by this Court inter alia contending that the construction of a garage has been made on the Government land attached to public road for which demolition notice has rightly been issued and the actions has rightly been taken. Learned Single Bench as well as Writ Appellate Court has refused to

jk/avi

interfere assigning the detailed reasons, therefore, there is no error apparent on the face of record in this case.

After hearing learned Counsel for the parties, the first argument advanced by the learned Counsel for the appellant do not attract in the present case because the said provisions are applicable in the cases where a person after purchasing a land construct a house on the road side. In such houses construction of garage is made compulsorily. It do not give right to them to construct the garage on Government land adjacent to public road, therefore, the said argument is wholly misplaced and cannot be countenanced.

So far as resume of the construction of garage of various persons on Government land are concerned, the said issue is not involved in the present case, looking to the nature of notice issued to the petitioner, therefore, we are not inclined to entertain the said point.

The issue regarding inherent defect in notice is concerned it is suffice to observe that construction of garage on the Government land situated road side is not permissible at all, therefore, we are not inclined to interfere in the order impugned in exercise of the power of Review in absence of any error apparent on the face of the order.

Accordingly, this Review Petition is dismissed with a cost of ₹ 25,000/- (Rupees Twenty Five Thousand). The amount be deposited to the Sikkim State Legal Services Authority within a period of 15 (fifteen) days from today.

Crl. M.C. No. 04/2014

3.It is stated in the petition that petitioners No. 1 and 2 were married in the year 1997 and they have two minor daughters from their wedlock.   A Criminal Complaint was filed on 23.11.2013 by petitioner No. 3 against petitioner No. 1 and on that basis an FIR No. 57/2013 was registered on 23.11.2013 under Section 498A IPC.  After completion of investigation, the police submitted a charge-sheet against petitioner No. 1 in the trial Court, where, it was registered as GR Case No. 09 of 2014.  It is also stated that during the pendency of the criminal case, parties have amicably settled their dispute and at present the petitioners No. 1 and 2 are residing together with their minor daughters.  Therefore, it has been prayed that further proceedings of GR Case No. 09 of 2014 be quashed.

They submitted that they have settled their disputes out of Court, the pendency of criminal case may create/develop bad relations between them, therefore, it will be proper to quash the criminal proceedings pending against petitioner No. 1. The parties have admitted their signatures and the contents of Deed of Compromise.

Crl. M.C. No. 04/2014

6.This Court in Mr. Tara Rai vs. State of Sikkim and another, Crl. M.C. No. 21 of 2013 decided on 12.12.2013, has considered the three-Judge Bench judgment of Hon’ble Apex Court in Gian Singh vs. State of Punjab & Another reported in (2012) 10 SCC 303 and held that although offence under Section 498A IPC is not compoundable, but if the parties have entered into a compromise, then it being a case arising out of matrimonial dispute, the proceedings of criminal case pending can be quashed.

[SECTION] ## 7.Paragraphs, 13, 14, 15 and 16 of the above referred Judgment are reproduced as under: -

“13.The larger Bench consisting of three-Judge of Hon’ble Apex Court in Gian Singh’s case (supra), considered a reference, referred by a two-Judge Bench, to see the correctness of the decisions of Hon’ble Apex Court in B.S. Joshi vs. State of Haryana : (2003) 4 SCC 675, Nikhil Merchant vs. CBI : (2008) 9 SCC 677 and Manoj Sharma vs. State : (2008) 16 SCC 1, wherein the Hon’ble Apex Court had permitted compounding of non-compoundable offences relating to matrimonial and civil disputes.  Hon’ble Apex Court in Gian Singh’s case (supra) considered its various judgments and also the judgment of five-Judge Bench of Punjab & Haryana in Kulwinder Singh vs. State of Punjab reported in (2007) 4 CTC 769 and a judgment of three-Judge Bench of the Bombay High Court in Abasahib Yadav Honmane vs. State of Maharashtra reported in (2008) 2 MAH LJ 856.  Hon’ble Apex Court considered the powers of High

Court under Section 482 of the Cr. P.C. and also provision of Section 320 Cr. P.C.

14.The Hon’ble Apex Court in Gian Singh’s case (supra) answered the reference and held that it cannot be said that B.S. Joshi, Nikhil Merchant andManoj Sharma cases (supra) were not correctly decided.    The Hon’ble Apex Court held that the power of the High Court in quashing a criminal proceeding or FIR or complaint in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction is distinct and different from the power given to a criminal court for compounding the offences under Section 320 of the Code.  In what cases power to quash the criminal proceeding or complaint or FIR may be exercised where the offender and the victim have settled their dispute would depend on the facts and circumstances in the case.

Court under Section 482 of the Cr. P.C. and also provision of Section 320 Cr. P.C.

14.The Hon’ble Apex Court in Gian Singh’s case (supra) answered the reference and held that it cannot be said that B.S. Joshi, Nikhil Merchant andManoj Sharma cases (supra) were not correctly decided.    The Hon’ble Apex Court held that the power of the High Court in quashing a criminal proceeding or FIR or complaint in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction is distinct and different from the power given to a criminal court for compounding the offences under Section 320 of the Code.  In what cases power to quash the criminal proceeding or complaint or FIR may be exercised where the offender and the victim have settled their dispute would depend on the facts and circumstances in the case.

15.It has further been held by Hon’ble Apex Court  that heinous and serious offences of mental depravity or offences like murder, rape, dacoity, etc. cannot be fittingly quashed even thought the victim or victim’s family and the offender have settled the dispute.  Such offences are not private in nature and have a serious impact on society.  But the criminal cases having overwhelmingly and pre-dominatingly civil flavour stand on a different footing for the purposes quashing, particularly, the offences arising from commercial, financial, mercantile, civil, partnership or such like transactions or the offences arising out of matrimony relating to dowry etc. or the family disputes where the wrong is basically private or personal in nature and the parties have resolved their entire dispute.  In this category of cases, the High Court may quash the criminal proceedings if in its view, because of the compromise between the offender and the victim, the possibility of conviction is remote and bleak and continuation of the criminal case would put the accused to great oppression and prejudice and extreme injustice would be caused to him by not quashing the criminal case despite full and complete settlement and compromise with the victim.   Paragraph 61 of the Gian Singh’s judgment is reproduced as under: -

“61. The position that emerges from the above discussion can be summarised thus: the power of the High Court in quashing a criminal proceeding or FIR or complaint in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction is distinct and different from the power given to a criminal court for compounding the offences under Section 320 ofthe Code. Inherent power is of wide plenitude with no statutory limitation but it has to be exercised in accord with the guideline engrafted in such power viz.: (i) to secure the ends of justice, or

[SECTION] ## Crl. M.C. No. 04/2014

“61. The position that emerges from the above discussion can be summarised thus: the power of the High Court in quashing a criminal proceeding or FIR or complaint in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction is distinct and different from the power given to a criminal court for compounding the offences under Section 320 ofthe Code. Inherent power is of wide plenitude with no statutory limitation but it has to be exercised in accord with the guideline engrafted in such power viz.: (i) to secure the ends of justice, or

[SECTION] ## Crl. M.C. No. 04/2014

(ii) to prevent abuse of the process of any court.In what cases power to quash the criminal proceeding or complaint or FIR may be exercised where the offender and the victim have settled their dispute would depend on the facts and circumstances of each case and no category can be prescribed. However, before exercise of such power, the High Court must have due regard to the nature and gravity of the crime. Heinous and serious offences of mental depravity or offences like murder, rape, dacoity, etc. cannot be fittingly quashed even though the victim or victim's family and theoffender have settled the dispute. Such offences are not private innature and have a serious impact on society.Similarly, any compromise between the victim and the offender in relation to the offences under special statutes like the Prevention of Corruption Act or the offences committed by public servants while working in that capacity, etc.; cannot provide for any basis for quashing criminal proceedings involving such offences. But the criminal cases having overwhelmingly and predominatingly civil flavour stand on a different footing for the purposes of quashing, particularly the offences arising from commercial, financial, mercantile, civil, partnership or such like transactions or the offences arising out of matrimony relating to dowry, etc. or the family disputes where the wrong is basically private or personal in nature and the parties have resolved their entire dispute. In this category of cases, the High Court may quash the criminal proceedings if in its view, because of the compromise between theoffender and the victim, the possibility of conviction is remote and bleak and continuation of the criminal case would put the accused to great oppression and prejudice and extreme injustice would be caused to him by not quashing the criminal case despite full and complete settlement and compromise with the victim. In other words, the High Court must consider whether it would be unfair orcontrary to the interest of justice to continue with the criminal proceeding or continuation of the criminal proceeding wouldtantamount to abuse of process of law despite settlement and compromise between the victim and the wrongdoer and whether to secure the ends of justice, it is appropriate that the criminal case is put to an end and if the answer to the above question(s) isin the affirmative, the High Court shall be well within its jurisdiction to quash the criminal proceeding.”

(Emphasis Supplied)

16.From the above, it is clear that Hon’ble Apex Court is specifically barred the compounding of the non-compounding offences in respect of heinous and serious offences mentioned in paragraph 61 of the judgment but allowed the High Court to quash the criminal proceedings, if in its view, on the basis of compromise of non-compoundable offences, where the offences arise from commercial, financial, mercantile, civil, partnership or such like transactions or the offences arising out of matrimony relating to dowry etc.or the family disputes where the wrong is basically private or personal in nature.”

8.Since, the present matter also arises out of matrimonial dispute and parties have entered into

Crl. M.C. No. 04/2014

(Emphasis Supplied)

16.From the above, it is clear that Hon’ble Apex Court is specifically barred the compounding of the non-compounding offences in respect of heinous and serious offences mentioned in paragraph 61 of the judgment but allowed the High Court to quash the criminal proceedings, if in its view, on the basis of compromise of non-compoundable offences, where the offences arise from commercial, financial, mercantile, civil, partnership or such like transactions or the offences arising out of matrimony relating to dowry etc.or the family disputes where the wrong is basically private or personal in nature.”

8.Since, the present matter also arises out of matrimonial dispute and parties have entered into

Crl. M.C. No. 04/2014

compromise, a written Deed of Compromise has been placed on record.  The parties are present in person and they have admitted their signature on Deed of Compromise and also the contents thereof.  In these circumstances, I am of the view that the ends of justice will meet in case the proceedings of the trial Court are quashed.

9.Consequently, this petition is allowed.  Further proceedings of GR Case No. 09 of 2014 State of Sikkim vs. Phuchung Tshering Bhutia, arising out of FIR No. 57/2013 dated 23.11.2013, pending in the Court of Judicial Magistrate (West) at Gyalshing are quashed and set aside.

10.A copy of this order be sent to the concerned Court for information and necessary action.

Sd/-

(N.K. Jain) Chief Justice 19.05.2014

[TITLE] # THE HIGH COURT OF SIKKIM  : GANGTOK(Criminal Jurisdiction)

[SECTION] ## DATED  :  7[th] OCTOBER, 2016

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[SECTION] ## S.B. :  HON’BLE M RS. JUSTICE M EENAKSHI M ADAN RAI, JUDGE

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[SECTION] ## Bail Appln.No.08 of 2016

Petitioner:Shri Jacob Rai (Khaling), Aged about 32 years, S/ o Shri Dal Bahadur Rai, R/ o Below Hotel Mayur, P.O. & P.S. Gangtok,  East Sikkim.Aged about 32 years, S/ o Shri Dal Bahadur Rai, R/ o Below Hotel Mayur, P.O. & P.S. Gangtok,  East Sikkim.

versus

[SECTION] ## Respondent:State of Sikkim

[SECTION] ## Application for Bail under Section 438  of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Appearance

Mr. Sudesh Joshi and Ms. Tengop Subba, Advocates for the Petitioner.

Mr. Karma Thinlay Namgyal, Additional Public Prosecutor with Mr. S. K. Chettri and Mrs. Pollin Rai, Assistant Public Prosecutors for the State on advance notice.

SI Silash Tamang, Investigating Officer, in person.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[SECTION] ## O R D E R

[SECTION] ## Meenakshi Madan Rai, J.

1. Heard.

2. Adverting to the allegations made out in the FIR against the

Petitioner, his Counsel in the first instance denies that the offence was at all committed by the Petitioner.  That, assuming but not admitting that

such an offence had been committed, no physical injury was caused to the Officers named in the FIR being Senior IAS Officers of the Government of Sikkim who for their part have not lodged any joint or individual FIR in connection with the incident, but has been lodged as an afterthought by the Station House Officer, Sadar Police Station, who was present at the place of occurrence, although no arrests were carried out at the spot.  That, he is the General Secretary of the principal Opposition Party in Sikkim, i.e., Sikkim Krantikari Morcha (SKM), and he along with his party members had expressed solidarity with former students of the Institute of Technology and Future Trends (ITFT), Chandigarh, who are agitating their demands in view of the non-recognition of their Degrees by the University Grants Commission, making them ineligible for higher studies, apart from which he has been raising issues on corruption in Sikkim.  A meeting was held on 21-09-2016 in the Conference Hall at Manan Kendra, Gangtok, with the Chief Secretary of the Government of Sikkim and the two Officers named in the FIR, on conclusion of which the students demanded copies of the minutes of the meeting, which were denied to them.  The students thus started raising slogans on which the Police intervened and forcibly removed them out of the Conference Hall and took them to Sadar Police Station.  It is urged that the Petitioner at no time manhandled any of the officials present, this being evident from the fact that although the Police were present at the Manan Kendra, the Petitioner was not arrested despite the alleged offence.  The acts of the Police officials are violative

Bail Appln. No.08 of 2016                                                            3

Bail Appln. No.08 of 2016                                                            3

of the provisions of the fundamental rights enshrined in Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India.   That, presently he is admitted in the Central Referral Hospital (CRH), Tadong, Gangtok, and undergoing treatment.  That, he is a permanent resident of Village Chumbung, Naya Bazar, West Sikkim, and apprehending arrest in connection with FIR dated 21-09-2016 under Sections 353/ 341/ 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short “ IPC” ) lodged by PI Bijay Subba, Station House Officer of the Sadar Police Station, Gangtok, following which Sadar Police Station Case bearing No.330/ 2016 dated 21-09-2016 has been registered against him.  He undertakes to cooperate with the Police in the investigation and that he is available at the Hospital for any information required from him.  It is prayed that this Court pass an order granting anticipatory bail.  To fortify his submissions, reliance was placed by Learned Counsel on the following decision;

(i)Siddharam Satlingappa M hetre vs. State of M aharashtra and Others :  (2011) 1 SCC 694  and Others :  (2011) 1 SCC 694

(ii)Shobhan Singh Khanka vs. State of Jharkhand : (2012) 4 SCC 684 SCC 684

(iii) Hema M ishra vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and Others : (2014) 4 SCC 453 4 SCC 453

(iv)Arnesh Kumar vs. State of Bihar and Another : (2014) 8 SCC 273 and 273 and

(v)Bhadresh Bipinbhai Sheth vs. State of Gujarat and Another: (2016) 1 SCC 152.  : (2016) 1 SCC 152.

Vehemently objecting to the submissions of Learned

3.

Counsel for the Petitioner, it was countered by Learned Additional

Bail Appln. No.08 of 2016                                                            4

Public Prosecutor that, the Petitioner is only seeking to draw political mileage of the entire situation as he is a member of the Opposition party and is inclined to give any agitation a political colour which likely will lead to a law and order situation.  That, the Petitioner had indeed committed the offence alleged in the FIR and custodial interrogation of the Petitioner is required as otherwise it is likely that he would tamper with witnesses.  Apart from that, the I.O. has to delve into questions of (i) whether the demand of the minutes of the meeting was made by the students or by the Petitioner (ii) whether the Petitioner was present at the meeting with the consent of the students or of his own accord and, (iii) ultimately the larger interest of the public has to be taken into consideration as a law and order situation could arise.  That, presently there is a Criminal Case pending against the Petitioner in the Sessions Court,  South  District  at Namchi, thereby indicative of the fact that he is a habitual offender. He relies on Bhagirath vs. State of M adhya Pradesh : 1981 (Supp) SCC 70 and K. K. Jerath vs. Union Territory, Chandigarh and Others : (1998) 4 SCC 80  and prays that this Application be rejected and dismissed.  A copy each of the Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (for short “ Cr.P.C.” ), statements of the Officers alleged to have been the victims have also been submitted before this Court.

4. I have heard the rival contentions of Learned Counsel and given due and anxious consideration to the same.  I have also carefully

perused the documents relied on by the parties and the citations made at the Bar.

5. I have given careful consideration to the Law relating to anticipatory bail as has been developed through the years by judicial interpretative process for which purpose I have meticulously perused the Judgements in Shri Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others vs. State of Punjab : (1980) 2 SCC 565, Siddharam Satlingappa M hetre(supra) and Bhadresh Bipinbhai Sheth (supra).  I have also perused the indepth discussions made under Section 41 of the Cr.P.C. in Arnesh Kumar (supra).

4. I have heard the rival contentions of Learned Counsel and given due and anxious consideration to the same.  I have also carefully

perused the documents relied on by the parties and the citations made at the Bar.

5. I have given careful consideration to the Law relating to anticipatory bail as has been developed through the years by judicial interpretative process for which purpose I have meticulously perused the Judgements in Shri Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others vs. State of Punjab : (1980) 2 SCC 565, Siddharam Satlingappa M hetre(supra) and Bhadresh Bipinbhai Sheth (supra).  I have also perused the indepth discussions made under Section 41 of the Cr.P.C. in Arnesh Kumar (supra).

6. Consequently, while considering a Petition under Section 438 of the Cr.P.C. what must, inter alia, weigh with the Court is the gravity of the offence, the severity of the penalty it entails and the requirement for custodial interrogation.  This, of course, has to be balanced with the possibility of the Petitioner seeking to impede investigation on which count the Courts ought to be circumspect.  In the instant matter, of the offences under which the Petitioner is booked, only one is a non-bailable offence which entails imprisonment for two years or fine or both.

7.It is not disputed that he has roots in society here, neither is there any apprehension on the part of the Prosecution that he will abscond so the question of his presence not being ensured during

Bail Appln. No.08 of 2016                                                            6

investigation or trial does not arise.  It would be relevant to notice that the FIR was lodged on 21-09-2016 with no arrest made till date, which thereby allays the apprehension of absconsion.  He is not guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life as the offence under Section 353 of the Cr.P.C. entails a two year imprisonment or fine or both as already discussed, in addition to which he undertakes to cooperate with the investigation in the matter.  The question of tampering with witness appears to be a little far-fetched as it is evident from the FIR that the students purportedly the witnesses in the case and the Petitioner do not appear to be at cross purposes, both having attended the meeting on a common agenda, i.e., on the point of non-recognition of the college degree as discussed supra. The allegation that he has criminal antecedents also boils down to a criminal case that is pending against him, the trial of which is still underway.

[SECTION] ## 8. In the aforesaid facts and circumstances and the discussions

herein, it is hereby Ordered that in the event of arrest of the Petitioner for the offences mentioned in the FIR, supra, he shall be released on bail on furnishing PB&SB of Rs.20,000/ - (Rupees twenty thousand) only, each, subject to the following conditions;

(ii)He shall not directly or indirectly make any inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of threat or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of

the Court or to any Police Officer.

10. The Application is allowed and stands disposed of accordingly.

THE KARMAPA CHARITABLE TRUST & ORS.

THE STATE OF SIKKIM & ORS.

[SECTION] ## O R D E R

1.Heard learned Counsel for the parties.

2.The Appellants are before this Court assailing the Order dated 30.04.2019 passed in Title Suit No. 1 of 2017 (Karmapa Charitable Trust & others v. State of Sikkim & others) by the Court of the learned District Judge, Special Division-I, Sikkim at Gangtok (I/C). The arguments advanced by learned Senior Counsel for the Appellants are that the learned trial Court vide the impugned Order dated 30.04.2019 did not consider it necessary to restrain the Urban Development and Housing Department (hereinafter “UD&HD”) from demolishing the Star

HIGH COURT OF SIKKIM                                                          Record of Proceedings

Cinema building in which the Appellants are shareholders inter alia on grounds that the Appellants are minority shareholders having a share holding of 0.66%. Moreover the compensation amount of Rs.3,69,788/- (Rupees three lakhs, sixty nine thousand, seven hundred and eighty eight) only, was issued in respect of the concerned share holding of the Dharma Chakra Centre (hereinafter “DCC”). As per the learned Senior Counsel,  the compensation amount was taken by the “Tshurpu Labrang,” who however is not a party in the instant matter. That, in fact this Court had declined to allow “Tshurpu Labrang” to be impleaded as a party earlier in time which therefore holds good. That, the learned trial Court has ordered that “Tshurpu Labrang”  file an Affidavit regarding the status of the said amount when it is a third party and is not a party to the instant proceedings and therefore the Order of the learned trial Court requires to be set aside and demolition of the property stayed.

3. Learned Government Advocate on the other hand submitted that the Government was unaware of the status of the “Tshurpu Labrang” and on the claim of one Tashi Wangyal claiming to be  the authorized representative of the said body had handed over the compensation amount of Rs.3,69,788/- (Rupees three lakhs, sixty nine thousand, seven hundred and eighty eight) only, to them. Admittedly, no documentary evidence was filed before the concerned Department to establish the authority of “Tshurpu Labrang.” Learned Government Advocate submits that steps are
